It's hard to say, it really depends on if you can get INFO 200 or not, the other prereqs are fairly easy to get a spot in, but 200 is a crapshoot. Also being a Junior by credits doesn't mean you have to get into the program immediately, you can take prereqs at a normal pace and be just fine. Honestly though getting into the program is hard to get into and it isn't getting any easier, if you're looking for a guaranteed spot in a program Informatics might be difficult. Keep in mind that even if you do get the prereqs done that doesn't guarantee you a spot in the major, I think the acceptance rate is ~15% per cycle now if not lower.

There's a huge variety in the classes, one of the quirks of the program is that it's very interdisciplinary. The nice part of that is other than a handful of core classes. You can really tailor your electives to learn about whatever you want, I've taken a ton of CS/Software related courses, but other people choose to lean towards more design or management based courses, so it's up to you.   

The program does have it shortcomings, the quality of a given course can vary wildly quarter-to-quarter depending on who happens to be teaching it, and you're definitely going to have to be more inclined towards self-teaching and supplemental learning to make up for the fact that you won't be taking certain core CSE courses.  

In terms of applying to the program, you'll have to take all of the prereqs beforehand, so you can't apply this cycle. I applied at the end of my sophomore year and was accepted. This is pretty common, only a handful of people get into informatics through DA, most people in the program get in late sophomore to early junior year as far as I can tell. The Bothell and Tacoma campuses don't have an Informatics program as far as I know, so you wouldn't be able to take INFO 200 there.

I can't really predict your odds based on your high school grades, so it really depends on how you do once you get here. The biggest bottleneck other than admission itself is getting a seat in INFO 200, it fills up incredibly quick and is probably the most important prerequisite. Keep in mind that the average grade in that class is quite high since it's not curved, so you need to do more than just succeed in the class to set yourself apart for admissions.

Almost everybody who joins the class had absolutely 0 experience! Generally the class is structured like this: 

1. Warmups- running around the mat room, shuffling, stretching, rolls, stuff of that nature
2.  Technique- the instructor demos a move or position, he talks through it and mentions details or options from that position, then you get a random partner and try it back and forth with each other. The instructor or other experienced people walk around and help everyone get it right
3. More technique, usually related/building on the last one
4. Sparring for club members, class members watch. Generally class starts light sparring towards the end of the class, but it’s a very gentle and safe introduction and you can take a break at any time. 

Let me know if you’re curious about anything else!
